items.title: Pig-butchering 2026: agentic AI grooming, approval-phishing drains, and Southeast Asia scam-centre strikes
items.summary: Pig-butchering has industrialised in 2026. Approval-phishing bypasses typical transaction monitoring; update typologies to flag repeated ERC-20 token-approval contract interactions from retail wallets. items.title: Treasury GENIUS Act tech report: AI-powered crypto oversight and a proposed 'digital-asset hold law'
items.summary: On 6 March 2026, Treasury published its congressionally-mandated report on innovative technologies to counter illicit finance in digital assets under the GENIUS Act. Treasury also signalled a nuanced shift on mixers, acknowledging legitimate privacy use cases rather than treating all mixer-touched funds as presumptively illicit.
items.soWhat: The proposed hold-law safe harbour removes a key legal barrier for proactive crypto intervention, directly reinforcing the on-ledger enforcement thesis already in Treasury's NPRM (see feed-treasury-programmable-enforcement). For bank compliance teams, the report is also a forward indicator for supervisory expectations: AI-assisted transaction monitoring and blockchain analytics are being positioned as required capabilities, not differentiators. The mixer nuance matters too — blanket mixer-flag policies may need recalibration against a mixed-use risk-based standard.

The absence of a kill-switch makes issuer-level sanctions structurally ineffective at stopping flows — the only reliable controls are blocking the fiat on/off ramps (Grinex, TengriCoin, Central Asian banking channels). Banks should treat any A7A5-denominated settlement or Grinex counterparty exposure as equivalent to direct Russia sanctions risk and prioritise on-chain screening of known A7A5 broker clusters.

items.title: FinCEN Section 311 severs Swiss MBaer Merchant Bank from US system — FINMA orders liquidation

items.title: CLARITY Act reaches US Senate floor calendar — 8 weeks to pass or die before summer recess
items.summary: The Digital Asset Market Clarity Act cleared the Senate Banking Committee 15–9 on 14 May 2026 and was formally placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar on 1 June 2026. The bill would resolve the SEC/CFTC jurisdiction standoff by routing every digital asset into one of three categories: digital commodities (CFTC exclusive jurisdiction), investment-contract assets (SEC), and permitted payment stablecoins (joint oversight). It faces a narrow runway — approximately eight weeks of Senate floor time before the summer recess — and needs 60 votes, requiring at least seven Democrats. The principal sticking point is an ethics provision mandating that the President and senior officials divest personal crypto holdings; without it, Democrats call the bill a dealbreaker. Galaxy Digital has reportedly bet $10M on 2026 passage.
items.soWhat: Passage would end five years of enforcement-by-litigation uncertainty on the securities/commodity classification question — materially reducing regulatory risk for US-facing crypto counterparties and reshaping what 'compliant' means for exchange and token products. Failure (or a thin partisan passage) leaves the SEC/CFTC ambiguity intact and signals continued litigation-as-regulation. Banks with US digital-asset exposure should treat the ethics-provision resolution as the leading indicator: a bipartisan deal implies durable certainty; a party-line result implies fragility.

items.title: Kroll: US AML fines declining as illicit crypto flows hit record $158B — deregulation widens enforcement gap
items.summary: Kroll's March 2026 report 'The Money Laundering Surge: Crypto, Enforcement Gaps and What Comes Next' documents a structural mismatch: crypto-linked illicit flows reached an estimated record $158 billion in 2025 — more than twice 2024's total — while global AML fines and penalties declined, especially in the US. Kroll attributes the enforcement gap to deregulatory trends, FinCEN staff reductions, and a fragmented state-level money transmitter licence framework that leaves crypto exchanges — handling trillions annually — subject to rarer and less rigorous federal examination than banks. AI-powered automation is identified as a key driver of the surge in laundering sophistication.
items.soWhat: A record illicit-flow number alongside declining US enforcement creates a de facto permissiveness signal that sophisticated laundering networks will exploit. For UK/EU institutions, the US enforcement gap means US-origin counterparties and correspondent flows warrant heightened scrutiny, not reduced, even as domestic US regulatory noise quietens under the Trump administration. The Kroll finding also validates the European approach of tightening (AMLA, MiCA) as a competitive differentiator — expect divergent standards between the US and EU crypto compliance regimes to widen further in 2026–27.

items.title: FBI IC3 2025: crypto fraud hits record $11.4B — half of all US cybercrime losses
items.summary: The FBI's 2025 Internet Crime Report (released 7 April 2026) recorded 181,565 crypto-related complaints totalling $11.4 billion, a 22% increase from 2024 and the highest annual figure on record. Crypto-linked losses now represent roughly 55% of the FBI's $20.9B total internet-crime loss tally. Investment fraud was the dominant sub-category at $7.2B; Americans over 60 accounted for $7.7B across all fraud types (up 37%). The report includes a first-ever AI-fraud section: 22,364 AI-related complaints at $893M. Operation Level Up — the FBI's proactive victim-notification programme using IC3 data to contact victims mid-scam — interrupted 3,780 cases in 2025 and saved an estimated $225.8M.
items.soWhat: Crypto-enabled investment fraud is now the largest single US cybercrime loss category by dollar value, and its share is growing. For banks, two operational implications follow: (1) transaction monitoring should be calibrated for higher SAR volumes from pig-butchering and trust-investment typologies as the loss curve steepens; (2) the $7.7B senior-loss figure creates specific obligations under financial-exploitation frameworks — front-line staff should treat rapid large crypto transfers by older customers as a red flag requiring positive confirmation of purpose. Operation Level Up's model also signals FBI expectation that financial institutions actively cooperate to interrupt fraud in progress, not just file retrospective SARs.

By early May 2026, 34 verified incidents had caused $101M+ in losses globally. Europe accounts for 82% of cases; France logged 41 kidnappings and home invasions since January — roughly one every 2.5 days — and has charged 88 suspects, more than 10 of them minors, across 12 active judicial investigations. Attackers are no longer opportunistic: transnational organised criminal networks use OSINT-driven targeting, social engineering, and extreme violence to extract private keys. CertiK projects 130+ incidents in 2026. Binance launched 'Withdraw Protection' in direct response.
items.soWhat: Physical coercion creates a laundering flow that bypasses most AML typologies — the victim authorises the transfer under duress, so on-chain it reads as a self-directed movement. For banks, proceeds may arrive as large rapid-liquidation flows from an account that appears to belong to the genuine holder. Typology update needed: flag high-value self-directed crypto transfers followed by rapid fiat off-ramp activity, particularly when preceded by unusual prior contact or OTC red flags. Relationship managers and branch staff should be briefed on distress signals. UK institutions face specific POCA obligations as receiving institutions for criminal property, regardless of whether the transfer looked voluntary.

Relationship-manager briefing on customer distress signals at point of instruction
Screen addresses linked to known wrench-attack clusters (CertiK Skynet)
Treat rapid large crypto liquidation from retail accounts as enhanced-due-diligence trigger
obligations: SAR on suspected theft proceeds transferred under duress
POCA obligations on receiving institutions for criminal property regardless of voluntary appearance

items.title: FCA CP26/13: cryptoasset perimeter guidance defines who needs FSMA authorisation from October 2027
items.summary: On 15 April 2026 the FCA published Consultation Paper CP26/13 adding a new Chapter 19 to the Perimeter Guidance Manual to clarify which activities require FCA authorisation under the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Cryptoassets) Regulations 2026, effective 25 October 2027. Seven regulated activities are addressed: issuing qualifying stablecoins, safeguarding cryptoassets, operating a trading platform, dealing as principal or agent, arranging deals, and arranging staking. The consultation closed 3 June 2026; final guidance is expected September 2026, ahead of the application gateway opening 30 September 2026.
items.soWhat: CP26/13 is the definitive guide to the UK crypto perimeter — it determines whether a counterparty, custodian or service provider will need FSMA authorisation. For banks, the critical sections are safeguarding and stablecoin issuance: firms that arrange safeguarding of qualifying cryptoassets for clients will need their own permissions, raising the authorisation bar for tokenised-asset custody and sub-custody arrangements. September 2026 final guidance will be the reference for counterparty authorisation-status assessments — banks should start tracking which CASP counterparties have engaged with PASS now, before authorisation status becomes determinative for relationship eligibility.

items.title: FCA publishes detailed AML/financial crime expectations for cryptoasset firms ahead of September 2026 gateway
items.summary: On 3 June 2026 the FCA published a webinar Q&A setting out its financial crime expectations for cryptoasset firms under the forthcoming FSMA regime. Key clarifications: no automatic conversion from MLR registration to FSMA authorisation; firms must satisfy materially higher standards — including MLRO competency, a documented and tested business-wide risk assessment (BWRA), justified and configured transaction monitoring tools, and end-to-end integration of AML, CTF, CPF and sanctions controls. The Travel Rule continues to operate concurrently under the MLRs and is assessed per firm. Applications open 30 September 2026.
items.soWhat: The FCA has raised the bar: FSMA authorisation requires full financial crime governance — not just AML registration. For banks, two direct implications: (1) any bank activity falling within the FSMA cryptoasset perimeter must plan a governance overhaul before September, not a registration renewal; (2) CASP counterparty assessments should use these expectations as the benchmark — a CASP that cannot demonstrate MLRO competency, a live BWRA and tested transaction monitoring is unlikely to pass the gateway, creating a forward-looking counterparty risk cliff from October 2027 for non-compliant firms.

items.title: New York DFS proposes GENIUS Act-compatible stablecoin framework — first state certification blueprint
items.summary: On 9 June 2026 the New York Department of Financial Services published a proposed regulation updating its USD-backed stablecoin framework to align with US Treasury's proposed requirements for state certification under the GENIUS Act. The proposal preserves NY's existing core requirements (full backing, redemption rights, independent audit) and adds federal provisions: custodian concentration limits (maximum reserves per single custodian) and mandatory risk management programmes covering internal controls, information security, internal audits, asset growth oversight, and affiliate transaction governance. A 10-day pre-proposal comment period opened June 9, followed by a 60-day formal consultation; the final rule takes effect when the GENIUS Act becomes effective, with a one-year transition for existing NY-licensed issuers.
items.soWhat: New York is the world's most experienced crypto supervisor — its GENIUS-compatible framework is the likely template for state certification across the US. The custodian concentration limits are significant: they impose portfolio diversification standards on reserve custodians, reducing single-point-of-failure risk. For banks, NY-licensed stablecoin issuers operating under this framework (including Circle's USDC) will offer stronger operational safeguards and a clearer compliance pathway than off-shore or non-certified issuers — a meaningful differentiator for counterparty risk tiering. Track the 60-day comment period; custodian limits and risk-management programme requirements are the provisions most likely to draw industry pushback.

items.title: 21 days to MiCA deadline: only ~17% of pre-MiCA VASPs licensed — banks face imminent CASP counterparty cliff
items.summary: With the MiCA transitional period expiring 1 July 2026, ESMA's Interim MiCA Register (refreshed 4 June) shows approximately 210 authorised CASPs against more than 1,200 pre-MiCA VASP entities — a ~17% conversion rate with three weeks remaining. Around 10 EU jurisdictions have issued zero CASP authorisations to date. An estimated 7.6 million of 18.5 million EU crypto app downloads in the past year went to currently unlicensed exchanges.
items.soWhat: Roughly 83% of the existing CASP universe will be operating in breach of EU law from July 1 unless they wind down or receive last-minute authorisation. For banks, any CASP counterparty relationship not confirmed as an authorised CASP in ESMA's register is a live compliance risk today — not a future risk. Run an immediate pass of all active CASP counterparties (including omnibus accounts, payment routing and liquidity providers) against the ESMA Interim MiCA Register. The 10 EU jurisdictions with zero authorisations signal uneven enforcement — monitor NCA-level post-July 1 actions. Existing item feed-mica-casp-july1-deadline covers the legal framework; this data quantifies the counterparty cliff.

items.title: GENIUS Act AML rule: Paradigm and Hyperliquid warn DeFi protocols could be swept into compliance perimeter
items.summary: As the FinCEN/OFAC GENIUS Act stablecoin AML/sanctions NPRM comment period closed on 9 June 2026, Paradigm and the Hyperliquid Policy Center submitted a joint letter arguing that the rule as drafted could treat stablecoin issuers as compliance gatekeepers for every downstream smart-contract interaction — including DeFi protocols the issuer does not control or monitor. They warned this could push regulated stablecoin activity offshore and unintentionally extend AML obligations to developers, validators, and protocol infrastructure builders. The final rule is expected later in 2026.
items.soWhat: The scope question — whether a stablecoin issuer's AML obligations follow the coin into permissionless DeFi — is now formally contested and will be resolved in the final rule. Two scenarios: (1) FinCEN confirms broad scope, forcing issuers to build real-time DeFi monitoring and potentially freezing coins used in non-compliant protocols — this would push DeFi toward regulated stablecoins with embedded compliance; (2) FinCEN excludes DeFi, leaving DeFi stablecoin flows in a grey compliance zone for bank counterparties. Banks with US stablecoin or DeFi exposure should monitor the final rule closely and refrain from assuming compliant stablecoin issuance extends compliance assurance into the DeFi layer.

items.title: US and Europol dismantle AudiA6 mixer — $389M laundered for ransomware gangs, two operators arrested
items.summary: On 11 June 2026, US authorities (DOJ Eastern District of Pennsylvania, IRS-CI, US Secret Service) and Europol dismantled AudiA6, a cryptocurrency mixing service that processed approximately $389M (EUR 336M) over five years, with at least $20M directly traceable to ransomware payments and dark-web criminal proceeds. Two operators — Igorevich Tkachuk, 37 (Ukraine), and Alexander Vladimirovich Ledenev, 25 (Russia) — were arrested in Batumi, Georgia. Europol linked AudiA6 infrastructure to 15+ international cybercrime investigations. Servers, domains, and encrypted assets were seized. Despite AudiA6's promises of untraceability, investigators traced transactions directly through exchange records.
items.soWhat: Two points for bank AML teams: first, mixer-based post-payment obfuscation remains active despite OFAC Tornado Cash sanctions — cross-chain and mixer-sequence typologies must stay live. Second, Europol's attribution of AudiA6 to 15+ cybercrime investigations means proceeds flowing through this service will surface in law-enforcement lookback requests — ensure your blockchain analytics tooling indexes the now-seized AudiA6 address clusters. The traceability finding (federal investigators traced every transaction despite 'untraceability' claims) also reinforces the operational value of on-chain forensics for mixer-touched flows.

items.title: FCA CP26/17: UK authorised funds may hold crypto ETNs up to 10% — first retail-fund crypto exposure rule
items.summary: Published 5 June 2026 (consultation closes 13 July 2026), FCA CP26/17 proposes that authorised UCITS and non-UCITS retail schemes (NURS) may hold cryptoasset exchange traded notes (cETNs) up to 10% of scheme property. Qualified investor schemes (QIS) face no cap; long-term asset funds (LTAFs) and feeder authorised investment funds (FAIFs) are excluded. The proposal follows the FCA lifting its retail cETN sales prohibition in August 2025 and sets the first explicit exposure limit for crypto within mainstream UK retail fund structures. CP26/17 also proposes setting regulated income as the tariff base for cryptoasset firms' FCA fees, and removing mandatory post-approval notifications for crypto financial promotions that are already substantially compliant.
items.soWhat: A 10% cETN cap in retail funds is a material boundary rule for UK fund managers and bank wealth platforms: existing and planned fund products must model crypto ETN allocations against the cap and assess liquidity risk under stress. For bank compliance, cETN holdings create a new AML/CFT due-diligence question — crypto-linked exposures in retail fund products may now feed into customer risk assessments. The regulated-income fee tariff is the first indicator of what FCA cryptoasset authorisation will cost, directly informing the build-vs-buy and counterparty-viability calculus for firms planning September 2026 gateway applications.
